title: Facial Nerve CN VII Anatomy: Branches, Taste & Pathways
description: Master facial nerve (CN VII) anatomy from the brainstem and temporal bone canal through the stylomastoid foramen to the five motor branches and taste path.
h1: Facial Nerve (CN VII) Anatomy: Intratemporal Path and Terminal Branches
blurb: Tracing Cranial Nerve VII from the pons through the temporal bone canal and parotid gland to its five facial expression branches, chorda tympani taste, and tear fibers.
lead: Every smile, blink, and raised eyebrow depends on the seventh cranial nerve—a complex mixed nerve that threads through the temporal bone before fanning across the face. In this illustrated guide to facial nerve CN VII anatomy, we examine 20 documented structures—including facial motor nucleus, nervus intermedius, internal acoustic meatus, geniculate ganglion—linking regional topography, tissue architecture, physiological mechanisms, and clinical reasoning.
overview: Every smile, blink, and raised eyebrow depends on the seventh cranial nerve—a complex mixed nerve that threads through the temporal bone before fanning across the face. CN VII contains motor fibers to muscles of facial expression, taste from anterior two-thirds of tongue (via chorda tympani), and parasympathetic pathways for lacrimal, submandibular and sublingual glands. It enters the internal acoustic meatus, bends at geniculate ganglion, traverses the facial canal and exits at stylomastoid foramen. Within the parotid it forms a motor plexus giving temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical branches; it passes through the gland but does not provide its secretomotor supply. Within the human body, the facial nerve · cn vii (Nervus facialis) is situated in pons → internal acoustic meatus → facial canal → stylomastoid foramen → parotid plexus, receives arterial perfusion via AICA/labyrinthine and petrosal branches intracranially; stylomastoid artery distally, and is innervated by CN VII motor, parasympathetic and taste fibers; cutaneous face sensation mainly CN V.

Structurally, the facial motor nucleus (Nucleus nervi facialis) comprises motor cell bodies in pons send axons looping around abducens nucleus before exit. Physiologically, the facial motor nucleus controls muscles of facial expression. Structurally, the nervus intermedius comprises sensory and parasympathetic root accompanying the motor root. Physiologically, the nervus intermedius carries taste and secretomotor pathways. Structurally, the internal acoustic meatus (Meatus acusticus internus) comprises temporal-bone canal shared by CN VII, CN VIII and labyrinthine artery. Physiologically, the internal acoustic meatus governs conveys nerve toward facial canal. Structurally, the geniculate ganglion (Ganglion geniculi) comprises sensory ganglion at first sharp bend of facial canal; greater petrosal branch arises nearby. Physiologically, the geniculate ganglion houses sensory neuron cell bodies. The greater petrosal nerve (Nervus petrosus major) carries preganglionic fibers toward pterygopalatine ganglion. Physiologically, the greater petrosal nerve supports lacrimal and nasal/palatine gland secretion. Structurally, the nerve to stapedius (Nervus stapedius) comprises branch in facial canal to stapedius muscle of middle ear. Physiologically, the nerve to stapedius governs dampens stapes movement.

Clinically, regarding the facial motor nucleus, upper face often retains bilateral cortical input in supranuclear lesions. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the nervus intermedius, explains why CN VII is not solely motor. In clinical pathology involving the internal acoustic meatus, lesions here may affect facial movement and hearing/balance. Medical evaluation of the geniculate ganglion also notes that herpes zoster may affect geniculate region.

questions.question: Which non-motor functions does the facial nerve carry?
questions.answer: The facial nerve carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and parasympathetic fibers to lacrimal, submandibular and sublingual glands.

questions.question: Does the facial nerve provide most facial skin sensation?
questions.answer: No. Most facial skin sensation travels through branches of the trigeminal nerve (CN V).

questions.question: What is the facial motor nucleus?
questions.answer: The facial motor nucleus is a group of pontine motor neurons whose axons loop around the abducens nucleus before exiting the brainstem.

questions.question: Where is the internal acoustic meatus located?
questions.answer: The internal acoustic meatus is a canal in the petrous temporal bone that transmits cranial nerves VII and VIII and the labyrinthine vessels.

questions.question: What is the function of the greater petrosal nerve?
questions.answer: The greater petrosal nerve carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibers toward the pterygopalatine ganglion, supporting lacrimal and nasal/palatal gland secretion.
